entry.evidence: the exact causes of this optical phenomenon in agates are still unclear and strongly depends on the geological specificity of the extraction site

steps.action: Pose the question of what causes the white and purple-blue banded colours of Yozgat agate, to be answered by combining XRD, Raman, LA-ICP-MS, UV-Vis-NIR and SEM.
steps.quote: The aim of this study is to provide an explanation of the origin of banded colours of Turkey purple-blue agate

steps.action: Take the rival explanations of agate colour and banding from the literature: chemical control by pigmenting impurities, Rayleigh scattering from submicrometric inclusions (Zolensky et al.), and scattering from fine chalcedony fibres (Deer et al.).
steps.quote: The characteristic rhythmic colour banding seems to be largely chemically controlled, reflecting variations in the deposition of pigmenting impurities.

steps.action: Measure the gemmological properties (refractive index, density, UV fluorescence) of the cabochon and record a bulk XRD pattern of the crushed rough sample, identifying quartz plus minor moganite reflections in the 18-32° range.
steps.quote: presents peaks ascribable to silica polymorphs, specifically quartz and moganite

steps.action: Confirm the phase identification with a second technique, confocal micro-Raman, which also shows only quartz and moganite.
steps.quote: Importantly, neither XRD nor Raman analyses register the presence of phases other than quartz and moganite.

steps.action: Compare quartz-normalised Raman spectra from blue and white bands and find a stronger 501 cm−1 moganite peak in the blue bands.
steps.quote: bluish stripes have a more intense moganite peak with respect to white stripes

steps.action: State the rival reading that the 501 cm−1 difference reflects SiOH content rather than moganite abundance, deferring its test to the NIR hydroxyl overtones.
steps.quote: changes in the peak at 501 cm−1 may be originated also by different content of SiOH groups

steps.action: Set the moganite-in-darker-bands result beside the same behaviour reported for agates from Permian basalts.
steps.quote: The same behaviour has been observed in other agates found in Permian basalt rocks showing moganite accumulation in the darker regions

steps.action: Acquire a Raman line map perpendicular to the bands (one spectrum every 2 µm), which confirms that the moganite/quartz ratio tracks the bands and shows quartz accumulation at band boundaries.
steps.quote: The line map (Fig. 3b) confirms that the ratio follows a trend related to the bands.

steps.action: Convert the moganite/quartz intensity ratio range (about 20-60%) to a moganite content of about 50-75 wt% using a published calibration (Götze et al. 1998).
steps.quote: This range corresponds to a moganite content of the order of 50–75 wt%

steps.action: Compare the moganite content with published moganite-age relations and with Eocene volcanic agates, and find agreement.
steps.quote: our results are in good agreement for agates found in volcanic rocks formed in Eocene period

steps.action: Measure trace-element concentrations by LA-ICP-MS at four points on white and on blue bands.
steps.quote: Table 1 summarises the average value of the concentrations of trace elements measured by LA-ICP-MS

steps.action: Compare white and blue band compositions: the differences concern only non-chromophore ions, and Al, Ti and Fe are similar; the values are also checked against Başıbüyük (2018) for the same region.
steps.quote: the small but statistically significant variations between the white and blue areas concern only ions that do not cause significant colouration in quartz

steps.action: Record in-line and diffuse UV-Vis-NIR absorption spectra, showing a scattering tail, hydroxyl overtones at 1425, 1900 and 2250 nm, and a broad absorption band centred near 570 nm that is resolved in diffuse geometry.
steps.quote: Superimposed to the scattering tail a minor shoulder contribution can be distinguished at about 500 nm.

steps.action: Attribute the 570 nm band to Fe-related colour centres of the amethyst type, by its position and width compared with published amethyst spectra.
steps.quote: the observed characteristics of the 570 nm peak in our sample is in agreement with Fe-related colour centres of amethysts

steps.action: Measure the absorption band at low temperature (13 K) with a cryocooler; the band is nearly unaltered, with a minor blue-shift and area increase that match the literature behaviour of amethyst.
steps.quote: examining the absorption peak collected at low temperature (inset of Fig. 4a), which basically remains unaltered with respect to room temperature measurement

steps.action: Compare diffuse absorption spectra taken on blue and on white bands of the cabochon and find them very similar, with intensity differences attributed to local thickness.
steps.quote: It is evident that the two spectra are very similar

steps.action: Exclude two rivals: that the band colours come from different colour-centre concentrations, and that the Raman 501 cm−1 difference comes from SiOH content (hydroxyl content is similar in the two bands).
steps.quote: the apparent band coloration is not due to different concentration of colour centres

steps.action: Propose that a nano- or microstructural characteristic controls the diffuse to in-line transmission ratio and hence the band tint.
steps.quote: The change of colour is, therefore, controlled by some nano- or microstructural characteristic

steps.action: Image HF-etched white and blue bands by SEM and find crystallites of about 5 µm in the white bands and about 300 nm in the blue bands.
steps.quote: The particle dimensions in the white zones are about 5 µm, while in the blue ones is about 300 nm.

steps.action: Apply the Apetz and Van Bruggen birefringent-scattering model, assuming equal Δn, to predict about 16 times greater Mie scattering losses in the white bands; invoke the λ^-4 Rayleigh law for the blue tint.
steps.quote: the expected scattering losses for the white part will be about 16 times greater than those of the blue zone

steps.action: Keep the explanation that Fe-related colour centres combine with grain-size-controlled scattering: Mie scattering dominates in the white bands, while in the blue bands the Fe peak and Rayleigh scattering prevail.
steps.quote: the unique purple-blue shades typical of Yozgat agates are a combination of iron-related colour centres and scattering effect

tree.answer: White and purple-blue banding in Yozgat chalcedony; phenomenon taken as given, not established
Colour is seen directly; its causes (phases, chromophores, grain size) need spectroscopy and SEM
Explain the atomic and microstructural origin of the band colours
Yes: chemical (colour-centre) control vs scattering; for the Raman peak, SiOH vs moganite
Chemical control predicts band-dependent chromophore content and absorption; structural control predicts the same absorption with different grain size
Set in the lab: band-resolved spot measurements and a low-temperature spectrum
Partly: XRD/Raman agreement, Raman line map, low-temperature spectrum; the scattering prediction is not measured per band
Combined Fe colour centres and grain-size-dependent scattering kept as best explanation

end.claim: The purple-blue banding of Yozgat agate arises because Fe-related (amethyst-type) colour centres are present at similar levels in all bands, while grain size (about 5 µm in white vs about 300 nm in blue bands) controls Mie versus Rayleigh scattering and so the perceived colour.

decisive_move.sentence: The band-resolved comparison of diffuse absorption spectra, showing no difference between blue and white bands, excluded colour-centre concentration as the cause and redirected the explanation to microstructure.

gates.evidence: Band-resolved Raman, LA-ICP-MS and absorption measurements were aimed at the question of chemical vs structural causes, but no hypothesis is stated before data collection. The SEM step is presented after the microstructural hypothesis, which may be narrative order (inference). The chemical-control rival could have been supported by band-dependent absorption and was not. The kept scattering explanation is supported only by a scaling estimate (16x) that is not compared with measured per-band in-line transmission. Nothing is reported as fixed in advance.

imports.item: Apetz and Van Bruggen (2003) light-scattering model for transparent polycrystalline alumina (scattering loss vs grain size and birefringence)
Rayleigh scattering λ^-4 law, citing an experimental verification of Rayleigh cross sections (Naus and Ubachs 2000)
NIST SRM 610 glass standard and the PerkinElmer TOTALQUANT semiquantitative protocol for LA-ICP-MS

limits: Sample base is small: one rough sample, one cabochon and one slab from a single dealer. LA-ICP-MS used four points per band, with a semiquantitative protocol and a single-standard correction. The paper calls the variations 'statistically significant' but describes no test. The kept scattering explanation rests on a scaling argument: it assumes equal Δn for quartz and moganite, and no measured per-band in-line or diffuse transmission ratio tests the predicted 16x difference. Rayleigh and Mie contributions are not separated quantitatively. Internal inconsistencies: the abstract places the absorption at about 500 nm, while the text says it is centred at 570 nm. The cabochon is about 5 mm thick in the text but 2-3 mm in the Fig. 4 caption. The Conclusions say moganite is 'possibly accompanied by differences in hydroxyl content', whereas the Results argue hydroxyl content is similar (inference: an editing inconsistency). Sub-claims and their statuses: moganite enrichment in blue bands is an observed pattern along one line map (regularity_in_range, single sample); moganite content of 50-75 wt% (estimate_with_resolution, coarse, via literature calibration); Fe-related amethyst-type colour centres (best_explanation, by spectral analogy plus low-temperature behaviour); grain sizes of about 5 µm vs 300 nm (direct observation, two SEM fields). Composition is none_fits: this is a single-specimen, multi-technique characterization that proceeds by elimination; the structural rival is formed after the chemical rival fails, not tested in a pre-designed crucial experiment. The one cited replication (Başıbüyük 2018) is a comparison with another group's data from the same region. No review file was supplied, so the review sequence is absent.

disagreements.target: Başıbüyük (2018), trace-element data for agate from the same Yozgat region
disagreements.support: The paper's LA-ICP-MS concentrations agree qualitatively but are one order of magnitude lower.
disagreements.quote: albeit our concentration is one order of magnitude lower

disagreements.target: Götze et al. (2001): rhythmic colour banding in agate is largely chemically controlled by pigmenting impurities
disagreements.support: For Yozgat agate, band-resolved absorption spectra and trace elements show similar chromophore content, so the banding colour is attributed to grain-size structure.
disagreements.quote: The origin of different colouration between bands is indeed caused by structural features and not by strong differences in the volumic number of colour centres.

disagreements.target: Schmidt et al. (2012, 2013): the 501 cm−1 Raman band may arise from non-bridging Si–OH rather than moganite
disagreements.support: Similar NIR hydroxyl overtones in blue and white bands are used to attribute the band-to-band 501 cm−1 differences to the moganite/quartz ratio.
disagreements.quote: mainly due to differences in the moganite/quartz ratio content rather than in Si–OH content

alternatives_considered.chosen: Band-dependent 501 cm−1 Raman intensity reflects the moganite/quartz ratio
alternatives_considered.reason: No strong differences in hydroxyl content from the near-infrared absorption features

alternatives_considered.chosen: Band colour controlled by nano- or microstructure
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Different concentration of colour centres between bands
alternatives_considered.reason: No appreciable changes in the shape and strength of absorption peaks in the transmitted diffuse light

alternatives_considered.chosen: Diffuse (integrating-sphere) geometry to resolve the 570 nm absorption band
alternatives_considered.reason: In in-line geometry the band is only a shoulder on the scattering tail; it 'can be fully appreciated' in diffuse geometry

alternatives_considered.chosen: Neglect refractive-index differences and assume equal birefringence Δn for quartz and moganite
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Phase-specific refractive indices and anisotropy (implied, not named)
